video_title: The AI "FOMO Feeding Frenzy" Is Here
gist: Dan Nathan interviews Amish, co-founder of New York VC firm First Mark, on whether the AI infrastructure buildout is a fiber-optic-style overbuild: the guest argues enterprise adoption is still in early innings so demand holds, but flags a post-transformer architecture shift as the under-discussed tail risk to Nvidia, OpenAI and Anthropic. He rejects the 'SaaS apocalypse' narrative, arguing value now rotates from infrastructure to the application layer, and predicts Anthropic/OpenAI IPOs would convert private-market 'FOMO feeding frenzy' scarcity pricing into fair public multiples and unlock trapped LP capital.

themes.theme: AI capex cycle vs. the fiber-optic overbuild

insights.claim: The AI platform shift is the fastest and largest-magnitude change this 20-plus-year enterprise VC has seen, and historical valuation/capital-raise comparisons are useless because every market got structurally bigger with each cycle (technology-for-technology's-sake, then software/cloud, then mobile, now economy-wide AI).
insights.speaker: Amish, co-founder First Mark
insights.so_what: Anchoring AI valuations to dot-com-era multiples or dollar levels will systematically mislead; size the opportunity off total economy exposure to labor/services automation instead.
insights.quote: this is the fastest change we've ever seen and of the largest magnitude

insights.claim: One bank projects $7 trillion of AI infrastructure spend by 2030, and the host frames this as the setup for an accident analogous to the late-1990s fiber-optic buildout where the application layer, not the infrastructure spenders, captured the economics.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: The fiber analogy implies the durable winners are the companies riding cheap post-bust capacity, not those funding it — a reason to underweight capex-financed builders relative to app-layer beneficiaries.
insights.quote: By 2030, I think one of the banks came out and said there's going to be seven trillion dollars spent on infrastructure. At some point, isn't there like an accident waiting to happen?

insights.claim: Enterprise AI adoption is still on the front end: Fortune 500/1000 firms have been slow and careful rolling out agentic capabilities because of security and related concerns, so a large wave of spend has not yet been placed.
insights.speaker: Amish, co-founder First Mark
insights.so_what: Supports staying long AI demand into any capacity scare; enterprise deployment timing, not model capability, is the near-term bottleneck to watch.
insights.quote: we're still on the front end of a massive amount of spend that is going to come through

insights.claim: The biggest and least-priced risk to the AI trade is a new algorithm or architecture that is far more cost-efficient than transformers, which would strand infrastructure built and sold out for the next eight years under the current regime.
insights.speaker: Amish, co-founder First Mark
insights.so_what: Argues against extrapolating current GPU/data-center demand five to seven years out; watch research conferences and world-model/recursive-intelligence work as the leading indicator of a hardware-requirement pivot.
insights.quote: what if someone comes up with a completely different algorithm that is way more costefficient? And what if we platform shift onto something else?

insights.claim: Biological intelligence is far more energy-efficient than transformer architectures, and mimicking it would produce breakthroughs in a completely different spend category than today's compute buildout — with quantum or biology cited as plausible sources.
insights.speaker: Amish, co-founder First Mark
insights.so_what: Frames the bear case for compute-levered names as an efficiency shock, not a demand shock — different hardware requirements would invalidate current capacity bookings.
insights.quote: the brain doesn't operate by transformer, you know, models, right? the brain operates in a very different way and it's incredibly energy efficient

themes.theme: Compute demand, model routing and neocloud supply

insights.claim: Companies like Shopify building their own internal coding agents to reduce reliance on OpenAI and Anthropic does not have to dent frontier-lab revenue growth, because token optimization and frontier-model saturation can grow simultaneously.
insights.speaker: Amish, co-founder First Mark
insights.so_what: Pushes back on the 'enterprises are churning off frontier models' short thesis for lab revenue; the shift is mix, not level.
insights.quote: I think people want an or answer and the likely result is an and

insights.claim: Very few companies will attempt true foundation-model training because of capital intensity — Apple has explicitly chosen to let others fight that battle and partner instead — while open-source models and routing layers like OpenRouter proliferate as every platform announces its own model-routing product.
insights.speaker: Amish, co-founder First Mark
insights.so_what: Routing/inference-optimization is a durable structural layer to own; the set of buyers of frontier training compute stays narrow and concentrated.
insights.quote: it's not a one-sizefits-all job

insights.claim: Nvidia is described as the most valuable company in the world running roughly 50% free cash flow margins, and its single biggest model risk is customer concentration giving one buyer leverage — which is why it is backstopping new neocloud entrants that could not otherwise get off the ground.
insights.speaker: Amish, co-founder First Mark
insights.so_what: Reframes Nvidia's vendor financing as deliberate customer diversification rather than demand-faking; concentration metrics are the number to track on Nvidia.
insights.quote: The biggest risk to their model is they somebody gets a lot of leverage over them. And when you have concentration in a couple of places, that's dangerous for them.

insights.claim: There are at least 250 neoclouds per Nvidia contacts, many arriving at First Mark's offices with backlogs of hundreds of millions of dollars, which the guest reads as real demand rather than paper capacity.
insights.speaker: Amish, co-founder First Mark
insights.so_what: Backlog quality across a fragmented 250-player neocloud field is the cleanest early-warning indicator for an AI capacity glut.
insights.quote: there's 250 Neo clouds at least maybe maybe more and so uh and yet a lot of them are seeing surging demand

insights.claim: Meta pivoting toward becoming a neocloud is read as capitulation after failing to ship a competitive open- or closed-source model, choosing instead to monetize already-purchased infrastructure the way Amazon did with AWS.
insights.speaker: Amish, co-founder First Mark
insights.so_what: Meta selling compute externally signals its internal model effort has underdelivered and adds another marginal supplier to the compute market.
insights.quote: I think there's a little bit of capitulation there

insights.claim: Circular AI financing is defended by analogy to AWS: Amazon exposed internal infrastructure to the market, ended up with a 45% operating-margin business, and supports its own competitors on it — so labs and chipmakers selling to and funding rivals makes the ecosystem healthier, though some of these circular arrangements should get unwound as the industry matures.
insights.speaker: Amish, co-founder First Mark
insights.so_what: A counter to the 'circular revenue' bear case, with the guest's own caveat that these structures are temporary — track unwinds as a maturity signal.
insights.quote: some of these things are circular and they're probably things that should get unwound over time as the industry matures

insights.claim: Anthropic is buying Google TPUs financed by alternative lenders — Blackstone and Apollo having just raised $35 billion — with the chips themselves securing the loans, meaning Anthropic funds purchases from the owner of its direct Gemini competitor.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Chip-collateralized private credit is the new marginal funder of AI capex; a demand pullback transmits into private credit books, not just equity.
insights.quote: the idea is that Anthropic is basically going to secure those loans with those exact chips

insights.claim: Capital-intensive neoclouds are the first businesses to fail on any demand pullback, and OpenAI's roughly $300 billion Oracle contract signed about a year ago would be at risk from delays or a demand air pocket, transmitting through component suppliers.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Oracle's RPO and neocloud credit are the highest-beta expressions of AI demand; watch contract delay disclosures as the first crack.
insights.quote: If you're Open AI and you gave Oracle a $300 billion contract about a year ago and there's any delays and then there's a pullback in demand, those contracts are done, right?

insights.claim: The compute shortage narrative flips abruptly rather than gradually, in the guest's formulation of how supply gluts arrive.
insights.speaker: Amish, co-founder First Mark
insights.so_what: Implies no gentle warning before an AI capacity glut — positioning must be adjusted ahead of, not during, the turn.
insights.quote: everything will seem like we are out of stock until we are completely in stock

themes.theme: Market positioning: semis lagging, software cut in half

insights.claim: At the time of recording the S&P 500 is making new all-time highs while the semis have not recovered nearly as much, with the semiconductor index having collapsed about 40% a couple of weeks earlier and the SOX still down roughly 25%.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: A divergence between record index highs and lagging semis is the cleanest tape-level evidence that AI leadership has broken; watch whether semis reclaim relative strength or the index follows them down.
insights.quote: And in general it's you know the socks is down about 25%. So there are some signs that maybe some of the stuff is getting um long in the tooth.

insights.claim: Legacy software has been repriced brutally, with Adobe down roughly 60%-plus from its all-time high and Salesforce still down about 50%, even as software has started to bounce.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Sets the entry-valuation backdrop for the guest's application-layer renaissance call — the disruption fear is already in these prices.
insights.quote: Adobe is down 60ome% from its all-time high. Salesforce is still down, you know, 50%

insights.claim: IBM's stock fell 25% the day after it disclosed that mainframe volumes were starting to get hit — used as evidence that legacy franchises persist for decades but are unforgiving when the last growth leg cracks.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan and Amish
insights.so_what: The trailing-edge customer base can support cash flows for 50 years, but the market pays nothing extra for it and punishes any decay — a template for how legacy SaaS gets valued.
insights.quote: The stock went down 25% the next day.

themes.theme: SaaS apocalypse rebuttal and the application-layer rotation

insights.claim: The benefit captured by infrastructure layers will transition to the application layer over the next decade because models have crossed a threshold of quality, dependability, harnesses and RAG that lets enterprises get assured outcomes — the front door of an application-layer renaissance.
insights.speaker: Amish, co-founder First Mark
insights.so_what: The core rotation call of the episode: fund flows from capex/infrastructure names toward vertical application software as deployment, not capability, becomes the constraint.
insights.quote: So I think I think we're actually going to come into a new renaissance era of the application layer and uh and we're on the very front doors of that.

insights.claim: The 'SaaS apocalypse' thesis is wrong because vibe-coded internal apps are buggy, untested and dependent on one or two employees who may leave, versus battle-tested software with thousands of customers and security assurance for $30,000-$40,000 — a fraction of one FTE.
insights.speaker: Amish, co-founder First Mark
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete price-vs-replacement-cost argument for owning oversold vertical SaaS; the buy-versus-build math still favors vendors at these price points.
insights.quote: or you can go with something that's what I call the software wisdom of the crowds like thousands of customers have run on it is secure it has been tested for security

insights.claim: The market's discount on large software incumbents reflects skepticism that they can retrain their people to behave like AI-native companies, and the re-rating signal is a new agentic product scaling from $1 million to $10 million inside a $200 million business, then $10 million to $75-100 million where it hits the top line and expands the multiple.
insights.speaker: Amish, co-founder First Mark
insights.so_what: A concrete revenue-scale tripwire for timing entry into de-rated software names — the multiple moves at the 10-to-100 leg, not the 1-to-10 leg.
insights.quote: that next go round of 10 to 75 or 100 that begins to show up in the top line that then shows up in the multiple

themes.theme: Incumbent M&A: distribution arbitrage, not mega-deals

insights.claim: No mega AI acquisition is expected because the breakout private companies are at $10 billion-plus valuations, AI companies can raise at 100 times revenue, and paying that multiple would hit the acquirer's stock through dilution — Salesforce trades at roughly its lowest multiple in 20 years.
insights.speaker: Amish, co-founder First Mark
insights.so_what: Do not position for transformative large-cap software M&A; the valuation gap between public acquirers and private AI targets structurally blocks it.
insights.quote: I don't see a big big deal on the horizon cuz I think the big companies are the ones that have broken out to the $10 billion plus uh valuation

insights.claim: Salesforce's actual playbook is quasi-private-equity distribution arbitrage: acquire $10-200 million revenue companies with real customer bases (not early technology) and push them through its channel to turn $10 million of revenue into $200 million in a quarter or two, with founders as potential successors — Brett Taylor being the original template.
insights.speaker: Amish, co-founder First Mark
insights.so_what: Sets the realistic deal-size band for Salesforce-style acquirers ($1-5 billion checks, $10-200 million revenue targets) — useful for handicapping takeout candidates.
insights.quote: that is a very much like a quasi private equity style playbook of like we can buy something, we can put it through our channel, we can pop the revenues

themes.theme: Private-market FOMO and the Anthropic/OpenAI IPO unlock

insights.claim: OpenAI and Anthropic reportedly both raised at $900 billion valuations — which would put them in roughly the top 25 of the S&P 500 — while public hyperscalers, software and semis sold off around 30% or more, implying the private marks would be cut in half if they traded publicly today.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Quantifies the mark-to-market gap on private AI marks; any lab IPO forces that gap to close and reprices every downstream private AI holding.
insights.quote: let's just call it they both raised at $900 billion

insights.claim: Anthropic and OpenAI are effectively forced toward public markets because the equity pool is exhausted — the most recent round raised more than the entire venture industry by a multiple in a single round, and even sovereigns are running out of money — after already raising tens of billions in debt.
insights.speaker: Amish, co-founder First Mark
insights.so_what: Frames a lab IPO as a funding necessity rather than a choice, which argues the offering comes whether or not the tape is receptive.
insights.quote: these guys in the last round raised more than the entire venture industry by a multiple in one round. The entire market, you know, you're running sovereigns are running out of money. Like, everyone's running out of money.

insights.claim: A trillion-dollar Anthropic valuation can be defended on approaching $100 billion of revenue growing three to four times year over year, which is about 10 times revenue — cheap relative to its growth even at that headline number.
insights.speaker: Amish, co-founder First Mark
insights.so_what: The bull frame for a lab IPO: 10x forward revenue on triple-digit growth, against a host counter that the company is simultaneously committing hundreds of billions in spend.
insights.quote: you're talking about a trillion dollar valuation, but all of a sudden, you hear the latest updates on the revenue and they're approaching a hundred billion and now you're looking at, well, geez, these guys are tripling and quadrupling year-over-year, maybe even more, and and you're paying 10 times

insights.claim: Private markets are a winner's-curse auction that produces a constant FOMO feeding frenzy and scarcity pricing; once SpaceX, Anthropic and OpenAI are public, pricing converts to a broad-based fair multiple, trapped LP capital creates selling pressure and rotation, and liquidity is released downstream to fund the next innovation wave.
insights.speaker: Amish, co-founder First Mark
insights.so_what: Anticipate persistent post-IPO supply from LP rotation out of the mega-names and a capital rotation into smaller/earlier AI stories once the scarcity premium collapses.
insights.quote: there is constantly this FOMO feeding frenzy

themes.theme: Where First Mark is deploying: agent security, sandboxes, vertical AI

insights.claim: First Mark is backing agent-runtime infrastructure: Onyx, which routes every agentic execution request through its product to verify intent and access rights, and Daytona, which spins up fast sandboxes so agents can run and then release resources at high performance.
insights.speaker: Amish, co-founder First Mark
insights.so_what: Agent security and ephemeral sandbox compute are emerging spend categories tied directly to enterprise agent rollout — capital-light picks-and-shovels on the adoption wave.

insights.claim: The firm's application-layer thesis is deeply vertical and data-driven — building harnesses and insights around how specific industries actually operate, such as payer-provider relationships in healthcare and marketing channel mechanics — because the last 24-36 months were experimentation and the market is now moving to durable enterprise-deployable capabilities.
insights.speaker: Amish, co-founder First Mark
insights.so_what: Vertical, context-owning AI applications are where this VC expects value to accrue next — the private-market analogue of the public application-layer rotation call.
insights.quote: we might have been for the last 24 36 months in the world of experimentation and trying lots of different things. Now we're going into durable uh capabilities that enterprises can deploy and use
